question.text: A trader holds 100 call options each with a delta of 0.5. How many units of the underlying bond must the trader sell to create a delta-neutral hedge?

explanation.text: The Logic: The total delta exposure of an option portfolio is the sum of (number of contracts x delta) across all positions. Here, 100 long calls x delta 0.5 = +50 deltas. Since each unit of the underlying bond has a delta of 1 by definition, selling 50 units (delta -1 each, total -50) brings the net position delta to zero, i.e., delta-neutral. The Trap: 100 units assumes each option has a delta of 1 (only deep-ITM options behave that way). 200 units doubles the required hedge incorrectly. 25 units halves it. Delta-neutrality requires offsetting the actual total option delta one-for-one with the underlying's delta. Note: The cited workbook (NISM Series IV, pages 137-138, 164-166, 192) supports delta as option-premium sensitivity and the positive delta of long calls — making the 100 x 0.5 = 50 arithmetic inferable — but does not explicitly cover delta-neutral hedge construction, the underlying's delta of 1, or the action of selling underlying units to neutralize call-option delta. The framing above is general option-Greeks/hedging knowledge.
